summary: The Internet Architecture Board (IAB) explains the architectural issues raised by Network Address Translators for IPv6, weighs their pros and cons, and gives its thoughts on open questions, in response to debate about whether the IETF should standardize IPv6 NATs. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: The Internet Architecture Board sets out why sites ask for address translation in IPv6 and what each reason actually costs. Its conclusion is that translation should not become a permanent part of the Internet, and that any solution should be judged on whether it keeps traffic reaching its destination without being rewritten in the middle.

questions: what does nat hide from an observer
subtitle: The IAB's position on network address translation in IPv6 and the trade-offs it creates.

tldr.problem: The IETF was debating whether to standardise network address translators for IPv6, and the argument turned on what translation actually buys a site and what it costs the wider Internet.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB lays out the properties sites want from translation, measures the obfuscation a translator can provide, and then asks the larger question: whether making translation a permanent part of the architecture is acceptable.
tldr.outcome: The IAB does not consider IPv6 NATs desirable, but accepts that some deployments are likely. It asks that any solution be judged on whether it keeps end-to-end transparency, so the real debate becomes how to confine translation's impact rather than whether to allow it.

today: RFC 5902 is an Informational document from July 2010, published by the Internet Architecture Board, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes it and none that updates it. It states the IAB's position on a question that was open at the time, and it notes that solutions to renumbering and multihoming were still an area of ongoing research and experimentation.

sections.title: The Debate About Standardizing IPv6 NAT
sections.content:
The IAB has published a number of documents about Internet transparency and the end-to-end principle. Most recently, RFC 4924 reaffirms those principles and reviews the documents in this area. They articulate the general principles the Internet architecture rests on, and the core values the community wants to protect.

Facing imminent IPv4 address space exhaustion, efforts to deploy IPv6 increased. Since late 2008 there have also been more discussions about whether the IETF should standardize network address translation within IPv6. People against it argue there is no fundamental need for IPv6 NAT, and that as IPv6 rolls out the Internet should converge on reinstallation of the end-to-end reachability that has been a key factor in the Internet's success. People for it argue that NAT vendors would provide IPv6 NAT implementations anyway, since translation solves a number of problems, and that the IETF should avoid repeating the mistake made with IPv4 NAT, where the lack of protocol standards led to different implementations and made NAT traversal difficult.

An earlier effort, RFC 4864, discusses the real or perceived benefits of NAT and suggests alternatives for most of them, with the intent of showing that NAT is not required to get the desired benefits. It also identifies several gaps remaining to be filled. This document gives the IAB's current thoughts on the debate, on the grounds that the question must be viewed from an overall architectural standpoint to assess the pros and cons of IPv6 NAT on the global Internet and its future development.
sections.plainLanguage: Two camps were arguing about IPv6. One said translation was not needed and that the Internet should go back to letting the two ends talk directly. The other said vendors would build it anyway, and that leaving it unstandardized would repeat the mess made of IPv4 translation. This document takes the argument above the level of features and asks what translation does to the architecture as a whole.

sections.title: What Sites Say They Want From Translation
sections.content:
Translation is seen as a way to achieve a number of desired properties for individual networks: avoiding renumbering, facilitating multihoming, making configurations homogenous, hiding internal network details, and providing simple security.

On avoiding renumbering: changing service providers with minimal operational difficulty matters in many networks, but renumbering is still painful today, as RFC 5887 discusses. It requires reconfiguring devices that deal with IP addresses or prefixes, including DNS servers, DHCP servers, firewalls, IPsec policies, and potentially many other systems such as intrusion detection, inventory management and patch management systems. In consumer networks such as home networks this is rarely a problem, because addresses or prefixes are typically obtained through DHCP and rarely configured by hand. In managed networks it can be serious. Many large enterprise networks avoid the problem by using provider-independent (PI) IP address blocks, but in smaller managed networks that cannot get PI blocks, renumbering remains a serious issue. Regional Internet Registries receive constant requests for PI blocks, and one main reason they hesitate to assign them to all users is concern about the impact of PI addresses on routing system scalability.

On site multihoming: a multihomed site essentially requires its IP prefixes to be present in the global routing table to get the reliability and load balancing it wants. Today, multihomed sites with PI addresses announce their PI prefixes to the global routing system, and multihomed sites with provider-allocated (PA) addresses announce the PA prefix they obtained from one service provider through another, effectively disabling provider-based prefix aggregation. This makes the global routing table scale linearly with the number of multihomed user networks. No solution except NAT has been deployed that insulates the routing system from the growing number of multihomed sites, where a multihomed site assigns multiple IPv4 addresses, one from each service provider, to its exit router, which is an IPv4 NAT box. Using translation this way has one unique advantage: no impact on routing system scalability, because the NAT box takes one address from each service provider and the site injects no routes of its own. The same solution could be rolled into IPv6, but it brings all the drawbacks of putting a site behind a NAT box, including the loss of reachability to the servers behind it. Announcing one's own prefixes achieves two further benefits: end-to-end communication survives the failure of an individual service provider as long as the site stays connected through at least one, and the site can perform traffic engineering and load balancing.

On homogeneous edge configurations: service providers supporting residential customers need to minimize support costs, and one key factor is ensuring customers have homogeneous configurations, including the addressing architecture. Today, when a service provider provides IPv4 NATs, all customers get the same address space on their home networks, so the home gateway always has the same address. From a customer-support perspective this may be the most important property of NAT usage today. In IPv6, link-local addresses can ensure all home gateways have the same address and give homogeneous addresses to other supported devices. Unlike IPv4, having a globally unique address does not prevent the use of a homogeneous address within the subnet. Only for multi-subnet customers would IPv6 NAT provide homogeneity that link-local addresses do not. Whether IPv6 link-local addresses give enough homogeneity to minimize help desk calls is currently unknown, and if they do not, providers might still want IPv6 NATs in the residential gateways they supply.
sections.plainLanguage: Three practical reasons come up for translation. It avoids the work of renumbering a network when the service provider changes, it lets a site use two providers without injecting its own routes into the global routing table, and it lets a provider give every home customer the same home gateway address, which makes support calls easier. Each of the three has a real cost attached to it.

sections.title: Hiding Hosts and Topology, and What That Costs
sections.content:
Most network administrators want to hide the details of the computing resources, information infrastructure and communications networks within their borders. This is rooted in the security principle that an organization's assets are for its sole use, and that information about those assets, their operation and the methods and tactics of their use are proprietary secrets. The first layer of protection is preventing access to those secrets or knowledge about them whenever possible.

Hiding hosts means keeping secret any information about the computer systems inside the network boundary, from workstations and laptops to servers, printers, scanners, IP telephones and point-of-sale machines. Administrators want to prevent an external entity from counting the number of hosts on the network, and they want to prevent host fingerprinting, which is gaining information about the constitution, contents or function of a host. Details that would aid an attacker include the operating system type and version, patches applied or not, the make and model of the hardware, and installed application software and its versions.

Host counting is hard to prevent. Bellovin showed how one can count the number of hosts behind a certain type of simple NAT box. More complex deployments, such as Network Address Port Translators (NAPTs) with a pool of public addresses randomly bound to internal hosts upon receipt of any new connection, without persistency across connections from the same host, are more successful at preventing host counting. The more complex the deployment, though, the less likely that complex connection types such as the Session Initiation Protocol (RFC 3261) and the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (RFC 4960) will traverse it.

Fingerprinting cannot be prevented completely, even by a complex NAT. The way different hosts respond to different requests and sequences of events indicates the type of host, its operating system and version, and sometimes installed applications. Scanning tools initiate connections of various types across a range of addresses, observe what returns, and send follow-up messages until they have fingerprinted the host. If the tool sits outside the network boundary and passively records connection exchanges, it can fingerprint hosts only if it can tell which externally visible connections come from the same internal host. With simple and static translation, where each host's internal address always maps to the same external address, the tool has 100% success. With a single external IP or a pool of dynamically assigned addresses assigned in a deterministic and predictable way, fingerprinting is more complex but quite achievable. With dynamically assigned addresses with short-term persistency and no externally learnable determinism, the problem gets harder: an observer may fingerprint a host during the lifetime of one address mapping, but once that mapping ends the observer does not know which new mapping is the same host. If temporal persistency is not deployed, this tactic becomes almost impossible. Deterrence of this kind comes at the cost of host reachability.

Topology hiding, meaning hiding the size of the network, the identities of internal routers and the interconnection among them, depends on the complexity, dynamism and pervasiveness of the bindings the NAT employs. Hiding actual addresses does not prove sufficient to hide internal topology: packet timing, delay measurements, the Hop Limit field or other header fields can reveal the relative distance between hosts. The degree of obfuscation a NAT achieves is a function of its complexity as measured by the use of one-to-many NAPT mappings, the randomness over time of the mappings from internal to external addresses, the lack of persistence of mappings, and the use of rewriting in IP header fields such as TTL. Deployers are warned: as obfuscation increases, host reachability decreases, and mechanisms such as STUN (RFC 5389) and Teredo (RFC 4380) fail with the more complex NAT mechanisms.

Simple security is the last claimed benefit. It is commonly perceived that a NAT box provides one level of protection because external hosts cannot directly initiate communication with hosts behind it. One should not confuse NAT boxes with firewalls. As RFC 4864 discusses, the act of translation does not provide security in itself. The stateful filtering function can provide the same level of protection without requiring a translation function.
sections.plainLanguage: Hiding the inside of a network is the reason many administrators want translation. The more a translator scrambles the view from outside, the harder it is to count or identify the machines behind it. But the same scrambling makes some kinds of traffic fail, and the benefit and the cost come from the same mechanism.

sections.title: Architectural Considerations of IPv6 NAT
sections.content:
It is important to distinguish the effects of a NAT box from the effects of a firewall. A firewall is intended to prevent unwanted traffic (RFC 4948) without impacting wanted traffic, whereas a NAT box also interferes with wanted traffic. In the rest of this section, reachability is used with respect to wanted traffic.

Discussions of IPv6 NAT often refer to the wide deployment of IPv4 NAT, where people have identified tangible benefits and gained operational experience. So far those discussions have focused on the potential benefits IPv6 NAT may bring, with little attention paid to the bigger picture. When considering the benefits IPv6 NAT may bring to a site that deploys it, the question must not be overlooked: if one site deploys IPv6 NAT, what is the potential impact on the rest of the Internet that does not? That means the Internet community that develops, deploys and uses end-to-end applications and protocols, and is affected by any loss of transparency.

The IAB puts the discussion in the context of the overall Internet architecture. The foremost question is not how many benefits one may derive from using IPv6 NAT, but whether a significant portion of parties on the Internet are willing to deploy IPv6 NAT, and hence whether the Internet wants to make IP address translation a permanent building block in the architecture. If transparency is not provided, making NAT a permanent building block would represent a fundamental architectural change.

It is desirable that IPv6 users and applications be able to reach each other directly without having to worry about translation boxes between the two ends. IPv6 application developers should be able to program on the assumption of end-to-end reachability of wanted traffic, without having to handle traversing NAT boxes. Referrals and multi-party conversations are straightforward with end-to-end addressing and vastly complicated in the presence of address translation. Network administrators should be able to run their networks without the added complexity of NATs, which brings the cost of extra boxes as well as increased difficulty in network monitoring and problem debugging.

Given the diversity of Internet user populations and of today's operational practice, it is conceivable that some parties have a strong desire to deploy IPv6 NAT, and the Internet should accommodate different views that lead to different practices. If some but not all parties want IPv6 NAT, then the real debate should not be about the benefits IPv6 NAT brings to the parties that deploy it. It is undeniable that translation can bring certain benefits to its users. The real challenge is how to design IPv6 NAT so that it can hide its impact within some localized scope. If that goal is achieved, the Internet as a whole can strive for reinstating the end-to-end reachability model.
sections.plainLanguage: A firewall and a translator are not the same thing. A firewall blocks what you do not want and leaves the rest alone; a translator also rewrites the traffic you wanted to send. That is why the IAB asks a question about the whole Internet, not about one site: if translation becomes normal, every application that assumes it can talk to the other end directly has to change.

sections.title: The Solution Space and the IAB's Recommendation
sections.content:
From an end-to-end perspective, the solution space for renumbering and multihoming can be broadly divided into three classes.

The first is endpoints getting a stable, globally reachable address. End sites use provider-independent addressing, so endpoints are unaffected by changing service providers. For this to be complete, provider-independent addressing must be available to all managed networks, that is, all networks that use manual configuration of addresses or prefixes in any type of system. In today's practice, assigning provider-independent addresses to all networks, including small ones, raises concerns about the scalability of the global routing system, and this is an area of ongoing research and experimentation.

The second is endpoints getting a stable but non-globally-routable address on physical interfaces, and a dynamic, globally routable address inside a tunnel. Hosts use locally scoped, and therefore provider-independent, addresses for communication within the site over their physical interfaces, so managed systems such as routers and DHCP servers all see stable addresses. Tunneling from the host to an infrastructure device is then used to communicate externally. This gives hosts globally routable addresses that may change, but the changes are confined to systems that operate over or beyond the tunnel, including DNS servers and applications, and those are often the systems that can already deal with changes today using mechanisms such as DNS dynamic update. If endpoints and the tunnel infrastructure devices are owned by different organizations, however, the solution is harder to deploy incrementally because of the incentive and coordination issues involved.

The third is endpoints getting a stable address that gets translated in the network. End sites use non-globally-routable addresses within the site and translate them to globally routable addresses somewhere in the network. In general this causes the loss of end-to-end transparency. If the translation is reversible, and it is indeed reversed by the time it reaches the other end, then end-to-end transparency can be provided. If the two translators involved are owned by different organizations, the solution is again harder to deploy incrementally because of the incentive and coordination issues involved.

On routing scalability, there is no immediate danger, but routing scalability has been a longtime concern in operational communities and an effective, deployable solution must be found. The question is not whether some parties can run NAT, but whether the Internet as a whole would be willing to rely on NAT to curtail the routing scalability problem, and whether all the potential impacts of doing so have been investigated to understand the cost on the overall architecture. If effective solutions can be deployed in time to allow provider-independent IPv6 addresses to be assigned to all user communities, the Internet can avoid the complexity, fragility and other unforeseen problems introduced by NAT.

RFC 4924 states that a network that does not filter or transform the data it carries may be said to be transparent or oblivious to the content of packets, and that networks providing oblivious transport enable the deployment of new services without requiring changes to the core. The IAB believes that providing end-to-end transparency is key to the success of the Internet. While some fields of traffic, such as Hop Limit, are defined to be mutable, transparency requires that fields not defined as such arrive untransformed. Currently the source and destination addresses are defined as immutable fields, and are used as such by many protocols and applications. Each of the three classes of solution can be defined in a way that preserves end-to-end transparency.

While the IAB does not consider IPv6 NATs desirable, it understands that some deployment of them is likely unless workable solutions to avoiding renumbering, facilitating multihoming without adversely impacting routing scalability, and homogeneity are generally recognized as useful and appropriate. It therefore strongly encourages the community to consider end-to-end transparency as a requirement when proposing any solution, whether based on tunneling or translation or some other technique. Solutions can then be compared on other aspects such as scalability and ease of deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three ways to solve the renumbering and multihoming problems without translation in the middle: give every site a permanent address of its own, keep the site's own addresses but reach the Internet through a tunnel that supplies a temporary global address, or translate the addresses somewhere in the network. The IAB's advice is to judge all three by one test: does the traffic still arrive with its original source and destination intact?

viz.caption: THE PROPERTIES SITES WANT FROM ADDRESS TRANSLATION

items.title: Avoiding renumbering
items.text: Changing service provider without reconfiguring every device that holds an address.

items.title: Facilitating multihoming
items.text: Using two providers without adding the site's own prefixes to the global routing table.

items.title: Homogeneous edge configurations
items.text: Every home gateway has the same address, which keeps support costs down.

items.title: Network obfuscation
items.text: Hiding the hosts, the topology and the number of machines inside the network.

items.title: Simple security
items.text: The belief that outsiders cannot start connections with hosts behind the box.

viz.caption: WHAT MAKES A TRANSLATOR HARDER TO OBSERVE

cells: Several internal hosts share external addresses
The same internal host does not keep the same external address
Mappings are short-lived and not reused
Rewriting header fields such as TTL
Some distance clues are removed from the packets

viz.caption: THE THREE CLASSES OF SOLUTION IN THE SOLUTION SPACE

cells: A provider-independent address that survives a change of provider
Giving one to every managed network raises concerns about routing scalability
Stable local address, dynamic address in a tunnel
A locally scoped address on the physical interface and a global one inside a tunnel
Harder to deploy incrementally when hosts and tunnel equipment have different owners
Stable address translated in the network
A non-globally-routable address inside the site, translated on the way out
Loses end-to-end transparency unless the translation is reversed at the far end
